case_studies.title: From Controlled to the Wild: Evaluation of Pentesting Agents for the Real-World
case_studies.abstract: AI pentesting agents are increasingly credible as offensive security systems, but current benchmarks still provide limited guidance on which will perform best in real-world targets. Existing evaluation protocols assess and optimize for predefined goals such as capture-the-flag, remote code execution, exploit reproduction, or trajectory similarity, in simplified or narrow settings. These tools are valuable for measuring bounded capabilities, yet they do not adequately capture the complexity, open-ended exploration, and strategic decision-making required in realistic pentesting. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of evaluating AI pentesting agents in real-world scenarios, building a more realistic evaluation protocol to test these agents, and resulting in a better understanding of their performance in complex environments. The researchers built a new evaluation framework that simulates real-world targets, allowing for more accurate assessment of AI pentesting agents. This research helps identify the most effective AI pentesting agents for real-world use.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage cloud security infrastructure, here is what to do: review your current pentesting tools and consider evaluating AI pentesting agents using a realistic evaluation protocol, assess their performance in complex environments, and adjust your security strategies accordingly. This flags a risk: if your org uses AI pentesting agents, check their performance in real-world scenarios immediately to ensure they are effective. Not directly applicable to non-security focused IT infrastructure work.
case_studies.score_reasoning: This paper shows novelty in evaluating AI pentesting agents in real-world settings. It's highly relevant to IT engineers working with security, and the paper offers actionable insights for building more effective pentesting agents within 90 days, thereby scoring high in value.

case_studies.title: MATRA: Modeling the Attack Surface of Agentic AI Systems -- OpenClaw Case Study
case_studies.abstract: LLMs are increasingly deployed as autonomous agents with access to tools, databases, and external services, yet practitioners (across different sectors) lack systematic methods to assess how known threat classes translate into concrete risks within a specific agentic deployment. We present MATRA, a pragmatic threat modeling framework for agentic AI systems that adapts established risk assessment methodology to systematically assess how known LLM threats translate into deployment-specific risks. MATRA begins with an asset-based impact assessment and utilizes attack trees to determine the likeli
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of assessing the attack surface of AI systems, specifically those using large language models, by building a threat modeling framework called MATRA. The result is a more systematic way to identify and mitigate risks in AI deployments. This framework helps organizations understand how known threats can impact their specific AI systems.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage AI or machine learning deployments, here is what to do: step 1, review your current risk assessment methodology, step 2, consider implementing MATRA to systematically assess deployment-specific risks, step 3, utilize attack trees to determine the likelihood of known threats.
case_studies.score_reasoning: High IT_RELEVANCE as it involves agentic systems and SaaS tooling. Novel approach to threat modeling, which could be valuable in real-world scenarios. Value in 90 days lies in applying the framework to existing LLM deployments to identify and mitigate potential risks. Novvity score moderate - while the specific LLM threat assessment framework and attack tree methodology are not new, the adaptation for agentic AI systems is novel.

case_studies.title: CppPerf: An Automated Pipeline and Dataset for Performance-Improving C++ Commits
case_studies.abstract: Recent progress in automated repair of performance bugs demands realistic, executable benchmarks. However, existing C++ performance benchmarks are largely built from competitive programming submissions, and recent real-world benchmarks predominantly target Python and .NET. To fill this gap, we present CppPerf-Mine, a configurable pipeline that mines execution-time-improving patches from open-source C++ repositories on GitHub by combining structural commit filtering, an LLM-based commit classifier, and a containerized build & test stage that produces fully reproducible Docker images for each pa
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of lacking realistic C++ performance benchmarks by building an automated pipeline called CppPerf-Mine, which mines execution-time-improving patches from open-source C++ repositories. The result is a dataset of performance-improving C++ commits. This research focuses on improving C++ code performance, which may not directly impact cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on improving C++ code performance rather than cloud infrastructure management or operations.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty: The combination of structural commit filtering, LLM-based commit classification, and containerized build & test stage is novel and surprising. IT_Relevance: Directly relevant to IT engineers working with C++ and performance optimization. Value_90_days: The automated pipeline and dataset can be used to improve C++ commit performance within 90 days.

case_studies.title: AssayBench: An Assay-Level Virtual Cell Benchmark for LLMs and Agents
case_studies.abstract: Recent advances in machine learning and large-scale biological data collections have revived the prospect of building a virtual cell, a computational model of cellular behavior that could accelerate biological discovery. One of the most compelling promises of this vision is the ability to perform in silico phenotypic screens, in which a model predicts the effects of cellular perturbations in unseen biological contexts. This task combines heterogeneous textual inputs with diverse phenotypic outputs, making it particularly well-suited to LLMs and agentic systems. Yet, no standard benchmark curre
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of lacking a standard benchmark for virtual cell models by building AssayBench, a virtual cell benchmark for machine learning models and agents. The result is a tool that can help predict cellular behavior and accelerate biological discovery. It is not directly relevant to cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty: The concept of an assay-level virtual cell benchmark for LLMs and agents is new, but lacks relevance to IT infrastructure. case_studies.title: Compute Where it Counts: Self Optimizing Language Models
case_studies.abstract: Efficient LLM inference research has largely focused on reducing the cost of each decoding step (e.g., using quantization, pruning, or sparse attention), typically applying a uniform computation budget to every generated token. In practice, token difficulty varies widely, so static compression can over-compute on easy steps and under-compute on hard ones. We study dynamic budget allocation for autoregressive decoding: learning how much computation to spend per token from within a single model. Self-Optimizing Language Models (SOL) pair a frozen LLM with a lightweight policy network that reads
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of inefficient computation in language models by dynamically allocating computation budget to each token, rather than applying a uniform budget. The researchers built a Self-Optimizing Language Model (SOL) that pairs a language model with a policy network to learn how much computation to spend per token. The result is a more efficient language model that can adapt to varying token difficulty.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage language model infrastructure, here is what to do: review your current language model deployment for opportunities to implement dynamic computation budget allocation, assess the potential benefits of integrating a policy network with your existing language model, and consider experimenting with SOL to improve efficiency and reduce costs.
case_studies.score_reasoning: The paper presents a novel approach to language model inference that could potentially improve efficiency and accuracy of LLMs. While the novelty of the approach is moderate, its direct relevance to IT engineers is high. However, the value 90 days ahead is low since implementing this would require significant changes to existing LLM architectures and may not be feasible within the given timeframe.

case_studies.title: Grounded Satirical Generation with RAG
case_studies.abstract: Humor generation remains challenging task for Large Language Models (LLMs), due to their subjective nature. We focus on satire, a form of humor strongly shaped by context. In this work, we present a novel pipeline for grounded satire generation that uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) over current news to produce satirical dictionary definitions in the Finnish context. We also introduce a new task-specific evaluation framework and annotate 100 generated definitions with six human annotators, enabling analysis across multiple experimental conditions, including cultural background, source-
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of generating satire using Large Language Models, building a pipeline that uses Retrieval-Augmented Generation to produce satirical dictionary definitions, with the result being a novel approach to humor generation. The research is specific to satire generation in the Finnish context. It does not directly affect IT infrastructure work.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on natural language processing for satire generation, which is not typically a concern for cloud infrastructure management.
case_studies.score_reasoning: Novelty score: The use of Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG) for satire generation is a new approach. However, the focus on Finnish context and dictionary definitions lowers the score. IT Relevance: This paper touches on LLM's capabilities but doesn't address real-world IT infrastructure directly. Value 90 Days: Although it's theoretically possible to apply this to humor generation in language models, it's not directly applicable to IT infrastructure.

case_studies.title: NanoResearch: Co-Evolving Skills, Memory, and Policy for Personalized Research Automation
case_studies.abstract: LLM-powered multi-agent systems can now automate the full research pipeline from ideation to paper writing, but a fundamental question remains: automation for whom? Researchers operate under different resource configurations, hold different methodological preferences, and target different output formats. A system that produces uniform outputs regardless of these differences will systematically under-serve every individual user, making personalization a precondition for research automation to be genuinely usable. case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of personalized research automation by building a system that can adapt to individual users' needs and preferences. The system, called NanoResearch, co-evolves skills, memory, and policy to automate the research pipeline. The result is a more usable and effective research automation system for users with different resource configurations and preferences.
case_studies.it_breakdown: Not directly applicable to IT infrastructure work, as it focuses on research automation and personalized systems for researchers, rather than managing cloud infrastructure or IT systems.

case_studies.title: SoK: A Systematic Bidirectional Literature Review of AI & DLT Convergence
case_studies.abstract: The integration of Artificial Intelligence (AI) with Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT) has become a growing research area, yet contributions tend to cluster around specific application domains or examine only one direction of the integration, leaving the broader architectural interplay between the two technologies poorly understood. case_studies.summary: This research reviews how Artificial Intelligence and Distributed Ledger Technology work together, solving the problem of a limited understanding of their integration. The authors built a systematic review of studies on AI and DLT convergence, resulting in a better understanding of how these technologies interact. This study helps identify potential applications and improvements for systems that use both AI and DLT.

case_studies.title: RUBEN: Rule-Based Explanations for Retrieval-Augmented LLM Systems
case_studies.abstract: This paper demonstrates RUBEN, an interactive tool for discovering minimal rules to explain the outputs of retrieval-augmented large language models (LLMs) in data-driven applications. We leverage novel pruning strategies to efficiently identify a minimal set of rules that subsume all others. We further demonstrate novel applications of these rules for LLM safety, specifically to test the resiliency of safety training and effectiveness of adversarial prompt injections.
case_studies.summary: This research solves the problem of explaining the outputs of large language models by building a tool called RUBEN, which discovers minimal rules to explain these outputs. The result is a more efficient way to identify a minimal set of rules that cover all others. This can help improve the safety of large language models.
case_studies.it_breakdown: If you manage large language models, here is what to do: review your current safety training, check for potential vulnerabilities to adversarial prompt injections, and consider using RUBEN to identify minimal rules that explain your model's outputs.
case_studies.score_reasoning: IT tools and systems are barely mentioned in the abstract, LLM-related. However novel pruning strategies may offer some potential for real-world improvement.
